### 🟡 Changes recommended Accepted precision values can collide with reserved metadata markers and produce unreadable zero-only pages.
1 open issue - [Reserved precisions make zero-only FLOAT/DOUBLE pages unreadable](https://github.com/apache/tsfile/pull/1024#discussion_r4303764720) · New
What changed in this PR Fixes #1020 by passing floating-point TS_2DIFF precision properties through C++ writer initialization. **Changes:** - Preserve schema properties and propagate them to value encoders. - Match Java precision parsing and NaN rounding behavior. - Add parser, encoder, and writer regressions. | File | Description | | ---- | ----------- | | cpp/​test/​writer/​ts2diff_precision_properties_test.cc | Tests precision across writer paths. | | cpp/​test/​encoding/​encoding_props_test.cc | Tests parsing, factory configuration, and rounding. | | cpp/​src/​writer/​value_page_writer.h | Declares property-aware initialization. | | cpp/​src/​writer/​value_page_writer.cc | Passes properties to value encoders. | | cpp/​src/​writer/​value_chunk_writer.h | Declares property-aware initialization. | | cpp/​src/​writer/​value_chunk_writer.cc | Forwards properties to value pages. | | cpp/​src/​writer/​tsfile_writer.cc | Preserves and propagates schema properties. | | cpp/​src/​writer/​page_writer.h | Declares property-aware initialization. | | cpp/​src/​writer/​page_writer.cc | Configures encoders with properties. | | cpp/​src/​writer/​chunk_writer.h | Declares property-aware initialization. | | cpp/​src/​writer/​chunk_writer.cc | Forwards properties to pages. | | cpp/​src/​encoding/​ts2diff_encoder.h | Handles NaN during integer rounding. | | cpp/​src/​encoding/​encoding_props.h | Adds Java-compatible precision parsing. | | cpp/​src/​encoding/​encoder_factory.h | Applies floating-point precision properties. |

comments.body: With `max_point_number=2147483646` or `2147483647`, a FLOAT/DOUBLE page containing only zeroes becomes unreadable even though writing succeeds. Infinite scaling produces NaN, which now rounds to zero and leaves every scaled flag set. Both floating-point `flush()` implementations therefore omit the bitmap wrapper and write the precision directly. These precisions are reserved overflow markers, so `read_page_meta()` treats the following block-header byte as a zero bitmap count and returns `E_DECODE_ERR`. Force the explicit bitmap wrapper for these reserved precisions in both flush implementations, and add zero-only round-trip regressions for both types and both precision values.

Confirmed by reproduction. On the published PR head, the added regressions fail in 32 zero-only writer variants plus one encoder boundary test. Both FLOAT and DOUBLE are affected, at precisions 2147483646 and 2147483647. The leading precision is interpreted as a bitmap marker, and C++ rejects the following zero count.

I have tested a local fix that forces the existing scaled-value bitmap wrapper for these two precisions, retaining an all-scaled bitmap and writing the actual precision after it. Both existing decoders understand that position as a precision value. The local fix passed 87 focused tests, 992 Windows tests and 1013 Linux tests. All 64 added C++ boundary pages were readable by Java; 8 additional C++ zero-only files passed both own and Java reads.

One compatibility detail: the current Java encoder itself emits unreadable zero-only pages for these two precisions (16 raw pages and 8 full files reproduced). Copying those bytes would reproduce the bug; the explicit existing wrapper is required. These invalid Java outputs are recorded as failures, not counted as interoperability passes.

The fix has not been pushed yet: our performance gate detected a small reproducible FLOAT record slowdown (125 paired runs, median ratio 1.0172, 95% CI [1.0062, 1.0244]). I am investigating that before publishing the revision and will update this thread with the validated commit and evidence.

The two reserved precision values now force the existing scaled-value bitmap wrapper in both floating-point flush paths, even when every value is scaled zero. The actual precision follows the count/bitmap and is read as a value by both existing decoders. Empty pages still emit nothing. The new zero-only regressions failed 33 tests before this correction and pass afterward.

The final revision also makes Java rounding exact at half-neighbors and large integers: the old `floor(x + 0.5)` can round twice. An IEEE-significand implementation matches Java on 1,088,975 deterministic random/edge inputs for both saturated int32 and int64 results (the legacy int64 floor approximation differs on 251). Actual NaN inputs keep the existing raw-bit handling; zero multiplied by an infinite scale rounds to zero. The record schema-check helpers borrow the caller-owned DeviceID instead of copying its shared_ptr on every record; they retain no reference and public APIs/object layouts are unchanged.

Final local validation:

- Original 122 page cases and another 122 cases with rounding boundaries: bidirectional decode and exact Java/C++ bytes all pass. Complete files: 64 original own/cross reads plus 16 additional C++ zero-file own/Java reads pass. Native compressed fixtures: C++ reads 135 Java files and Java reads 117 C++ files.

Of 48 valid Java boundary pages, 36 match raw bytes and 12 one-value pages differ only in the pre-existing unused zero-delta minimum field.
- Changed executable lines: 97/97 (100.00%); corresponding branches 44.78%, with no branch exclusions or ignored parse errors. Format and patch checks pass.

The earlier performance signal was investigated rather than omitted. Final paired latency ratios (same benchmark source/configuration, 125 retained pairs for FLOAT record including the fixed-size confirmation; 25 pairs for each other workload):
- `float_nonaligned_record_default`: 1.0000, 95% CI [0.9941, 1.0049].
- `double_nonaligned_tablet_default`: 0.9812, 95% CI [0.9662, 0.9901].
- `float_aligned_tablet_precision_2`: 0.9822, 95% CI [0.9756, 0.9868].

### 🟡 Changes recommended The scalar fallback can lose matching NULL rows and return nullable Boolean rows outside the time filter.
3 open issues - [Time pruning incorrectly skips NULL timestamp rows](https://github.com/apache/tsfile/pull/1026#discussion_r4305097605) · New - [NULL Boolean rows bypass time predicate filtering](https://github.com/apache/tsfile/pull/1026#discussion_r4305097623) · New - [All-NULL projected fields produce empty results](https://github.com/apache/tsfile/pull/1026#discussion_r4305097635) · New
What changed in this PR Addresses #1025 by evaluating FIELD predicates in C++ aligned table queries while preserving the unfiltered fast path. **Changes:** - Adds typed, NULL-aware row predicates and legacy callback dispatch. - Evaluates predicates before OFFSET/LIMIT and advances rejected rows. - Adds tests for types, NULLs, pagination, and callback errors. | File | Description | | ---- | ----------- | | `cpp/​test/​reader/​table_field_filter_test.cc` | Adds predicate and query regression tests. | | `cpp/​src/​reader/​filter/​table_field_filter.h` | Defines borrowed typed row views and predicate API. | | `cpp/​src/​reader/​filter/​table_field_filter.cc` | Implements typed and legacy predicate dispatch. | | `cpp/​src/​reader/​block/​single_device_tsblock_reader.h` | Declares FIELD evaluation helper. | | `cpp/​src/​reader/​block/​single_device_tsblock_reader.cc` | Integrates filtering into scalar row processing. |
Review effort: Balanced
Copilot was unable to review this pull request because the user who requested the review has reached their quota limit.

comments.body: The new per-column path can discard matching NULL rows before the FIELD callback. `AlignedChunkReader::cur_page_may_satisfy_filter()` requires both time-page and value-page statistics to match, but value statistics exclude NULL timestamps. For example, a page containing `(1,42), (2,NULL), (3,NULL)` in a multi-page chunk is skipped for `time >= 2`, so an IS NULL predicate never sees rows 2 and 3. Use time-page statistics for aligned time pruning, and add coverage for matching NULL timestamps outside the non-NULL value range.

The per-column path can return NULL BOOLEAN rows excluded by the time predicate. In `aligned_chunk_reader.cc:728–743`, the scalar Boolean decoder appends NULL rows and continues without checking that predicate. A page containing `(time=1, flag=NULL), (time=2, flag=true)`, queried with `time >= 2` and an accept-all `TableFieldFilter`, therefore emits both timestamps. Apply the time predicate to NULL Boolean rows before exposing them to FIELD evaluation or OFFSET/LIMIT accounting, and add a regression for this combination.

When every projected FIELD is all-NULL, this fallback never invokes the predicate. `construct_column_context()` skips aligned value indexes with `count_ == 0`, and `init_internal()` then returns an empty result because value indexes were requested. Projecting only the fixture's `empty` column with an accept-all or IS NULL `TableFieldFilter` therefore loses all 28 rows and callbacks. Preserve an aligned timestamp source for this case, and add a regression that projects only `empty`, without a non-NULL anchor field.

Confirmed. The aligned value page's time statistics exclude NULL entries, so they cannot rule out candidate timestamps in the shared time page. I reproduced this with `(t0,42),(t1,NULL),(t2,NULL)` and a time window `[t1,t2]`: the prior PR returned 0 rows, while Java and the corrected C++ return 4 across two devices, on either writer's file. Commit 249b0d51a6bfe202185aa21b794ff21ccdfafcf3 uses only shared time-page statistics for this conservative page check. Missing time statistics keep the page. The new test runs with row/batch-1/batch-4 and parallel on/off.

The revision also fixes the test-only TAG predicate leak behind the two Linux ASan CI failures: the query borrows this predicate, so it now has stack ownership. The old test reproduced 480 leaked bytes in six allocations; the revised Linux ASan/UBSan full suite passes with leak detection enabled.

Validation for 249b0d51a6bfe202185aa21b794ff21ccdfafcf3: all 24 added regression configurations fail on the old PR head and pass after the fix; 74 focused, 979 Windows Release, 1000 all-codec Linux, and 999 Linux ASan/UBSan full-suite tests pass. ## Updated: committed mask bulk copy and C++/Java selectivity benchmark

Measured on **October 22, 2026**, after committing and pushing `11bfc35c99f8e845939a6753f004ecee38c7a2ec` to PR #1026.

## Exact source and implementation

- **C++ revision: `11bfc35c99f8e845939a6753f004ecee38c7a2ec`**, committed and pushed. No uncommitted source patch is needed. The implementation bulk-copies contiguous selected mask runs for dense fixed-width columns, retaining NULL/string fallbacks and correct OFFSET/LIMIT, duplicate projection, extra time-column and source-block cursor behavior. - C++ uses native structured `AlignedFieldFilter`. Java uses the public `TableQueryExecutor` / `TsBlockReader` and applies the equivalent predicate to returned blocks. The current Java table API does not expose a directly usable equivalent structured FIELD-predicate contract. This compares **end-to-end filtered-query usage against a Java scan/filter reference**, not identical internal predicate pushdown plans, isolated decoding speed, or language performance in general.

## Data and queries

- One host: Apple M5 Pro, 24 GiB RAM, macOS 26.6.2.
- **2,000,000 aligned rows**, one device, eight INT64 FIELDs (`v0`…`v7`), no NULLs.
- Timestamp `r`; `v0 = (r * 1543 + 17) % 10000`; `vc = r * 8 + c` for `c = 1..7`.
- Predicate **`v0 < percentage * 100`** gives exact accepted fractions **0 / 1 / 10 / 50 / 100%**. Matches are distributed across pages, not a contiguous time prefix.
- Projection widths **1 / 4 / 8**: `v0` through `v(width-1)`.
- PLAIN values, TS_2DIFF time, UNCOMPRESSED; explicit flush every 100,000 rows; page limits 10,000 points / 128 KiB.
- Identical deterministic logical data generated independently by the C++ and Java writers. Both readers query **each exact same file**; these files are logically equivalent, not byte-identical. The input files are the frozen files from the earlier report; their writer implementations did not change in this commit. File sizes and SHA-256 values are recorded.

## Measurement and validation

**30 scenarios × 2 implementations × 5 fresh processes × 5 timed queries = 1,500 new timed samples.** None of the previous working-tree or paired-experiment timings are merged into this matrix.

Each process first executes one discarded exhaustive timestamp/order/row-count/projected-value validation query and two further discarded warm-up queries. Every timed query reopens its reader and verifies exact row count plus timestamp and all projected-value checksums. All scenarios pass; checksums match across readers and writer files.

Timing includes file open, metadata/query construction, scan/filter, consumption of selected timestamps and every projected value, and result/reader close. JVM startup, file generation, exhaustive validation and warm-up are excluded. Both use 1,024-row output blocks. The statistic is the **median of five process medians**, each over five timed queries. Ratio = Java reference median / C++ median; >1 means C++ is faster.

Cases are deterministically shuffled and implementation order alternated; measured processes do not overlap. This is a warm-OS-cache microbenchmark, not a cold-cache or tail-latency result.
